description: We are a team of Czech students passionate about space, technology, programming, mathematics, and data science. Our skills include Python, CSharp, JavaScript, data analysis, and software development. We enjoy solving complex problems and turning creative ideas into practical solutions. We're looking for curious, motivated teammates with skills in astronomy, physics, UI/UX design, or data visualization. Working remotely and online.
summary:
TerraSignal is an interactive web application that helps people investigate Earth system change using NASA data. Users can select a location, variable and period, visualize observations, estimate rates of change and assess statistical evidence through confidence intervals, significance tests and data coverage.
Our atlas presents 45 years of daily weather indices at 193 sampled NASA POWER model grid cells. Users can compare places, explore monthly and seasonal temperature and precipitation, and investigate hot days, frost days, warm nights and dry spells. Connections and Memory workspaces extend the investigation to soil wetness, MODIS vegetation greenness and responses to dry episodes.
TerraSignal addresses the challenge by showing what is changing, where, by how much and how confidently the selected record supports a trend. Original sources, missing observations and methodological limits remain visible, with downloadable evidence for further investigation. This helps students, educators and curious citizens explore environmental change while understanding uncertainty and avoiding unsupported causal claims.
details:
TerraSignal is an interactive web application that helps students and curious members of the public investigate environmental change using NASA Earth data. Our goal is to make long environmental records easier to explore, understand and question. Users can investigate familiar places, compare locations and distinguish an unusual year from a persistent trend.

The application combines maps, interactive charts and guided investigations. Its saved atlas covers 1981–2025 and shows hot days, frost days, warm-night proxies and the longest dry spell within each year at sampled locations. Users can switch between annual values, departures from a fixed 1991–2020 reference and long-term trends. They can also select additional coordinates, retrieve records, explore monthly and seasonal patterns, and compare two places. Saved examples provide a quick starting point without requiring another NASA download.

We use NASA POWER for temperature, precipitation and root-zone soil wetness, and NASA Terra MODIS MOD13Q1 vegetation data, accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer, to examine vegetation greenness. The backend validates records, preserves missing observations and calculates historical trends. Monthly trend models account for seasonal differences, while uncertainty estimates allow for correlation between observations. Defined groups of trend tests receive multiple-testing corrections. Users can inspect coverage, units, source URLs and retrieval dates, then download data and analysis evidence as CSV or JSON.

A creative part of TerraSignal is its “Landscape Memory” investigation. It follows dry episodes through rainfall, soil wetness and vegetation records, allowing users to examine whether these records return to typical conditions at different times. It also invites users to challenge the claim that every dry episode includes both low soil wetness and low vegetation greenness. Users can inspect counterexamples, compare threshold choices and see when missing data prevent a conclusion. This makes scientific questioning part of the experience.

We built the frontend with React, TypeScript, HTML and CSS, using Vite for development and builds. Leaflet displays the interactive OpenStreetMap basemap. The backend uses Python and FastAPI, with HTTPX for data requests and NumPy, SciPy and statsmodels for numerical and statistical analysis. Git and GitHub support collaboration, and Docker packages the application for deployment. OpenAI Codex assisted development, code review and documentation. The project runs in a web browser and requires no custom sensors or specialized hardware.

Our team considered scientific validity, ease of use, accessibility, reproducibility and the reliability of external data services. Guided questions, keyboard controls and clear explanations help users navigate the analysis. Caching and saved records reduce repeated downloads. We also make spatial and scientific limits explicit: weather grid cells and satellite sampling areas have different footprints, correlations do not establish causes, and vegetation greenness alone cannot establish ecosystem recovery. The intended impact is stronger environmental data literacy—helping users ask meaningful questions, assess evidence and communicate uncertainty. Further scientific review and user feedback are planned to evaluate and improve that experience.
